prompt: A cookie was set on Monday. What makes it appear in a request on Friday?
hint: Ask what decides to attach it.

choices.text: A script on the page reads it
choices.why: No code is involved; a cookie is attached with the page unaware.

choices.text: The browser, with the page unaware
choices.why: Set once, returned for ever, with nothing deciding.

choices.text: The server asks for it again
choices.why: There is no second asking; the first response was the whole arrangement.

choices.text: A background task renews it
choices.why: Nothing renews it; storage and attachment are the same simple rule.

prompt: A site keeps two kilobytes of preferences in a cookie. What does that cost?
hint: Think about how many requests a page makes.

choices.text: Two kilobytes of browser storage
choices.why: True, and the storage is not what the cost is about.

choices.text: Two kilobytes uploaded sixty times
choices.why: A hundred and twenty kilobytes nobody wanted to send.

choices.text: A delay while it is written
choices.why: Writing it is immediate; it is the repeated sending that adds up.

choices.text: A second request to fetch it
choices.why: There is no separate fetch; a cookie travels in the request headers.

prompt: Fill the blank: a cookie set by something embedded in the page and loaded from elsewhere — an advertisement, an analytics script — is called a ___-party cookie.
hint: First-party is the site in the address bar.

prompt: Which of these does the browser check before attaching a cookie? Choose all that apply.
hint: Three tests, and the ones left out are why the attributes exist.

choices.text: Whether the request is going to the site that set it
choices.why: The default, and it is narrow on purpose.

choices.text: Whether the path is under the cookie’s `Path`
choices.why: A tidiness feature rather than a security one.

choices.text: Whether it has expired
choices.why: An expired cookie is dropped rather than sent.

choices.text: Which page caused the request to be made
choices.why: Precisely what the default rules leave out, and what `SameSite` was added for.

choices.text: Whether the request came from a click or from a script
choices.why: Also not checked by default, and also part of the forgery problem.

prompt: A visitor suddenly gets a `400` about a header being too large, on every page of one site, and the site works for everybody else. What happened?
hint: Something has been accumulating in their browser.

choices.text: Their cookies for the site are too large
choices.why: Clearing them fixes it instantly, which few visitors discover.

choices.text: The server has run out of memory
choices.why: That would affect everybody rather than one person on every page.

choices.text: Their browser sends a corrupt header
choices.why: Corruption would be intermittent; this is on every page.

choices.text: A page sets a cookie past the limit
choices.why: A single oversized cookie is refused by the browser rather than sent.

prompt: What does `HttpOnly` do?
hint: It is about what can read the value, not about who receives it.

choices.text: It hides the cookie from page scripts
choices.why: The browser keeps sending it and refuses to show it to the page.

choices.text: It keeps the cookie off plain HTTP
choices.why: That is `Secure`, and the names are close enough to be worth separating.

choices.text: It blocks cross-site requests
choices.why: That is `SameSite`, which answers a different attack entirely.

choices.text: It stops the cookie reaching disk
choices.why: That is what leaving out an expiry does, and it has another name.

prompt: Match each attribute to what it closes.
hint: Three attacks and one convenience.

pairs.right: The value crossing the network in the clear
An injected script reading the value
Another site’s page causing an authenticated request
A session that outlives its usefulness

right_distractors: A visitor editing the value by hand
A cookie growing past the size limit

prompt: Why is `SameSite=Lax` the common choice rather than `Strict`?
hint: Think about arriving from an email.

choices.text: `Strict` is refused by some browsers
choices.why: Browsers accept it; the objection is about what it does when accepted.

choices.text: A link from elsewhere arrives signed in
choices.why: `Strict` would send no cookie, so the visitor lands signed out.

choices.text: `Strict` requires `Secure`
choices.why: That requirement belongs to `None`, and for a different reason.

choices.text: `Lax` also covers background requests
choices.why: Backwards: `Strict` is the tighter of the two on background requests.

prompt: Fill the blank: a cookie whose name begins with `__Host-` is refused by the browser unless it is Secure, has `Path=/`, and carries no ___ attribute at all.
hint: It is the one that widens a cookie to subdomains.

prompt: What is the risk of widening a cookie to every subdomain?
hint: Ask who runs the least careful subdomain.

choices.text: Subdomains serve stale values
choices.why: The browser sends the same value to each; there is nothing to go out of date.

choices.text: The cookie is sent twice
choices.why: It is one cookie and it is sent once.

choices.text: The weakest subdomain reads it too
choices.why: And a subdomain left pointing at a provider can be claimed by a stranger.

choices.text: It counts against each subdomain's limit
choices.why: The limit is per cookie, and widening does not multiply it.

prompt: Why does the cookie hold an identifier rather than the visitor’s name and role?
hint: Four benefits, and one of them is about ending a session.

choices.text: Browsers refuse personal values
choices.why: The browser stores any text and has no opinion about its meaning.

choices.text: It means nothing, so it cannot be edited
choices.why: And the row behind it can be deleted, which ends the session at once.

choices.text: Names and roles change
choices.why: True of the data and not the reason; the identifier would go stale the same way.

choices.text: The browser routes the cookie by it
choices.why: That is decided by the cookie’s domain, not by the value.

prompt: A site issues session identifiers that count upwards. What is the attack?
hint: It needs no skill and no tools.

choices.text: An attacker tries the neighbouring numbers
choices.why: Found in production systems of every size.

choices.text: An attacker counts the visitors
choices.why: A real leak of information, and far less serious than being signed in.

choices.text: The browser refuses a value that is a number
choices.why: The browser stores it happily; the value’s shape means nothing to it.

choices.text: Two visitors share an identifier
choices.why: A counter would give them different numbers; that failure comes from elsewhere.

prompt: Fill the blank: issuing a new session identifier at the moment the visitor signs in closes an attack called session ___.
hint: The attacker chose the value in advance.

prompt: Logging out clears the cookie and nothing else. What is still true afterwards?
hint: Ask which of the two copies is the session.

choices.text: Signed out here, the row works elsewhere
choices.why: Anybody who copied the value earlier is unaffected by the clearing.

choices.text: The session ends next request
choices.why: A missing cookie looks like a new visitor; the row is left untouched.

choices.text: The row goes at its idle timeout
choices.why: The gap lasts the whole timeout, which is exactly the window that matters.

choices.text: The browser notifies the server
choices.why: Clearing a cookie is a local act and sends nothing anywhere.

prompt: A site keeps its session table in the memory of one server, and a second server is added. What do visitors see?
hint: Ask what happens when a request lands on the other machine.

choices.text: Slower pages, two tables to check
choices.why: Nothing checks two tables; a server knows about its own and no other.

choices.text: They are signed out at random
choices.why: Half their requests reach a machine that has never heard of them.

choices.text: Sessions that last twice as long
choices.why: Neither machine has the other’s rows, so nothing is duplicated.

choices.text: A warning from the browser itself
choices.why: The browser has no way to notice and would have no reason to complain.

prompt: What does signing a token prevent?
hint: One of the two verbs. Not the other.

choices.text: Anybody reading what is inside
choices.why: The contents are readable after a decoding step that needs no key.

choices.text: It being changed and not detected
choices.why: Signed is not encrypted; treat the contents as a postcard.

choices.text: It being used elsewhere
choices.why: A signature says nothing about where the token is presented from.

choices.text: It being replayed after expiry
choices.why: The expiry is checked separately, and it is inside rather than enforced by the signature.

prompt: Somebody’s access is withdrawn and they hold a valid token. What happens?
hint: Ask what the server checks it against.

choices.text: It keeps working until it expires
choices.why: There is no row to delete; every server reaches yesterday's conclusion.

choices.text: The next server refuses it
choices.why: Looking the account up is the lookup the arrangement exists to avoid.

choices.text: It stops; the key was rotated
choices.why: Rotating the key would invalidate the tokens of everybody at once.

choices.text: The browser discards it
choices.why: Nothing reaches into the browser, which is the shape of the whole problem.

prompt: Fill the blank: short-lived tokens are paired with a longer-lived ___ token, and refusing that one is how access is withdrawn.
hint: It is used to obtain a new short one.

prompt: Which of these are true of keeping a credential in local storage? Choose all that apply.
hint: One of these is the reason the arrangement is riskier than it looks.

choices.text: There is no equivalent of `HttpOnly` for it
choices.why: Which is the whole of the objection.

choices.text: Any script running on the page reads everything in it
choices.why: Including a script that arrived inside a third-party library.

choices.text: Your own code has to attach it to each request by hand
choices.why: The browser attaches cookies and not this.

choices.text: The browser sends it automatically to the site that stored it
choices.why: It sends nothing; that is the difference from a cookie.

choices.text: It is refused on connections that are not encrypted
choices.why: Local storage has no such rule; that is the `Secure` attribute of a cookie.

prompt: Early libraries read the algorithm from inside the token and used whatever it named. What went wrong?
hint: The sender controls that part of the token.

choices.text: The algorithms named were slower
choices.why: Speed was not the issue; belief was.

choices.text: Tokens saying 'none' were believed
choices.why: The verifier decides the algorithm; what arrives may be checked, never obeyed.

choices.text: Services disagreed on the algorithm
choices.why: An interoperability annoyance, and not the failure this describes.

choices.text: The name added bytes to each request
choices.why: A cost, and nowhere near the seriousness of the actual defect.

prompt: A response said `max-age=3600` and it was fetched ten minutes ago. What happens on the next request for it?
hint: Ask whether anything leaves the machine.

choices.text: A conditional request and a `304`
choices.why: That is what happens after the hour, when the copy has gone stale.

choices.text: No network activity of any kind
choices.why: Nothing leaves the machine and no server log records it.

choices.text: It is fetched from scratch anyway
choices.why: A fresh copy is used without asking; that is what fresh means.

choices.text: The copy is used, checked behind
choices.why: That behaviour exists and has to be asked for by name.

prompt: What does `no-cache` instruct a cache to do?
hint: The name is the trap.

choices.text: Store it nowhere
choices.why: That is `no-store`, and the two names are worth memorising apart.

choices.text: Keep a copy, check before use
choices.why: Which gives a `304` on most requests and correct content on every one.

choices.text: Keep it for the shortest period
choices.why: There is no such period; the instruction is about asking rather than about time.

choices.text: Keep it and use it, unless reloaded
choices.why: That describes what a reload does, and it is not what this directive says.

prompt: Fill the blank: a conditional request that finds nothing has changed is answered `___ Not Modified`, with no body at all.
hint: Three hundred and something.

prompt: A page showing somebody’s order history is sent with `Cache-Control: public`. Why is that serious?
hint: Ask which caches are now allowed to keep it.

choices.text: A shared cache serves it to somebody else
choices.why: Invisible to whoever is testing on their own machine.

choices.text: The page is kept much longer than intended
choices.why: Staleness is decided by the age directives, not by this word.

choices.text: The browser refuses to store it
choices.why: `public` widens who may keep it rather than narrowing it.

choices.text: Search engines index the page
choices.why: Indexing is decided elsewhere entirely and is unrelated to this header.

prompt: What does `stale-while-revalidate` change?
hint: Think about who waits.

choices.text: The stale copy is served, then refreshed
choices.why: Nobody waits for a revalidation; the next visitor gets the new version.

choices.text: The copy stops going stale
choices.why: It still goes stale; what changes is what happens at that moment.

choices.text: A stale copy is served when the server is down
choices.why: That is `stale-if-error`, which covers a different bad minute.

choices.text: Revalidation is spread across visitors
choices.why: A wait is not divisible; one request either waits or it does not.

prompt: A stylesheet was sent with a year-long cache and is now wrong. What reaches the visitors who already have it?
hint: The same shape as the permanent redirect from the last lesson.

choices.text: A purge at the CDN edge
choices.why: A purge empties the CDN and reaches no browser at all.

choices.text: Nothing that you serve
choices.why: They are not asking, so there is nothing to answer.

choices.text: A response to their next request
choices.why: A fresh copy is used without a request, which is the whole difficulty.

choices.text: An update once the browser notices
choices.why: Nothing compares anything while the copy is still fresh.

prompt: Why does a fingerprint in a built file’s name make a year-long cache safe?
hint: Ask what a new build produces.

choices.text: The browser checks the fingerprint
choices.why: Nothing checks it; the name is an address and the browser reads it as one.

choices.text: That content is fixed; a change renames it
choices.why: Nothing is invalidated: the old name simply stops being mentioned.

choices.text: Caches revalidate any hashed address
choices.why: No such rule exists, and requiring it would defeat the purpose.

choices.text: The browser keeps one copy per fingerprint
choices.why: Eviction is the browser’s own business and is not driven by the name.

prompt: Fill the blank: hashed files are served with `max-age=31536000, ___`, and that second word stops even a reload from revalidating them.
hint: It says the content will not change.

prompt: If everything else is cached for a year, what has to stay short-lived?
hint: Something has to carry the new names.

choices.text: The page that names the other files
choices.why: Small, changed on every deploy, and usually answered `304`.

choices.text: The largest file
choices.why: Size has nothing to do with it; the entry point does.

choices.text: Anything an interface returns
choices.why: Often true, and it is a separate decision from the one being asked about.

choices.text: The fonts
choices.why: Browsers apply no such limit to fonts.

prompt: Why do caching defects rarely reproduce for whoever is investigating them?
hint: Ask what is in that person’s browser.

choices.text: They are testing a different build
choices.why: A deploy is not what differs; the stored copies are.

choices.text: Their browser holds nothing old
choices.why: The affected people visited a week ago and have not been back.

choices.text: Their network is faster
choices.why: Speed has no bearing on whether a fresh copy is used.

choices.text: The developer tools disable compression
choices.why: Compression is unrelated, and that setting is not what differs here.

prompt: Choose the attributes for the cookie that says who a visitor is.
hint: Four decisions, and each closes something real.

choices.text: `Secure`, `HttpOnly`, `SameSite=Lax`
choices.why: The combination, and none of it costs anything to write.

choices.text: `Secure` alone, with SameSite left unset
choices.why: That value reopens the forgery this was built to close.

choices.text: `HttpOnly` alone
choices.why: `Secure` and `SameSite` both apply to a first-party session cookie.

choices.text: `Path=/admin` on its own
choices.why: A tidiness feature, and no substitute for any of the three.

prompt: A bank’s statement page should be sent with which instruction?
hint: One of them declines to keep anything.

choices.text: `no-store`
choices.why: Nothing is written down, which is the point on a shared machine.

choices.text: `no-cache`
choices.why: A copy still exists on disk, which is what is being avoided.

choices.text: `private, max-age=0`
choices.why: Close, and a copy still exists; stale is not the same as absent.

choices.text: `public, max-age=60`
choices.why: A shared cache is now holding one person's statement.

prompt: Match each thing to what it is stored in.
hint: Two of them live in the browser.

pairs.right: The browser’s cache, under a hashed name

pairs.left: Whether a copy is still current
pairs.right: An ETag, compared on a conditional request

prompt: Fill the blank: HTTP remembers nothing between requests, so state is added on top by giving the browser something to send back — a ___.
hint: The subject of the first half of this lesson.

prompt: Which of these end a session for somebody who copied the cookie value earlier? Choose all that apply.
hint: Ask which act reaches the server’s table.

choices.text: Deleting the row on the server
choices.why: Every copy of the value becomes worthless at once.

choices.text: Reaching the absolute timeout
choices.why: The row stops being valid whatever holds the value.

choices.text: Refusing the refresh, in a token arrangement with short lifetimes
choices.why: Access ends within the lifetime of the short token.

choices.text: Clearing the cookie in the visitor’s browser
choices.why: A local act that leaves the row alive and reachable.

choices.text: Setting `HttpOnly` on the cookie afterwards
choices.why: It changes what a script may read and revokes nothing.

prompt: A page with sixty resources is visited a second time, and all of them are fresh. How many requests go out?
hint: Fresh means something specific.

choices.text: Sixty, each answered `304`
choices.why: That is the stale case; fresh copies are used without asking.

choices.text: None; the network is idle
choices.why: The page assembles from disk before the network is consulted.

choices.text: One, for the page itself
choices.why: Close, and it depends on the page's own instruction rather than on freshness.

choices.text: Sixty, all revalidated
choices.why: A fresh copy is used without any revalidation.

prompt: An embedded widget on somebody else’s site stops being able to see its own cookie. What is the likely reason?
hint: Its cookie is third-party there.

choices.text: The browser restricts embedded cookies
choices.why: A schedule somebody else controls, and it has been running for years.

choices.text: Its server now rejects requests with no referrer
choices.why: A plausible fault, and it would not present as a missing cookie.

choices.text: The host site set the same name
choices.why: Cookies of different sites are kept apart and do not overwrite each other.

choices.text: The cookie is over the size limit
choices.why: The limit applies per site, so the two piles are counted separately.

prompt: A cookie of 2 kilobytes is attached to each of a page’s 60 requests. How many kilobytes is that, uploaded, for one page view?
hint: One multiplication.

prompt: Put the steps of a conditional request in order.
hint: It begins after the stored copy has gone stale.
items: The stored copy passes its freshness time
The browser sends what it has as a fingerprint
The server compares it against the current content
A `304` comes back with no body, and the copy is fresh again
trap: The tempting order puts the server's comparison first, because that is where the decision is made. The browser has to send the fingerprint before there is anything to compare, and it only does so once the copy has gone stale.

prompt: Which arrangement lets you sign somebody out within a second of deciding to?
hint: Ask what the credential is checked against.

choices.text: A signed token of fifteen minutes
choices.why: That is fifteen minutes rather than a second, which is the known trade.

choices.text: A session identifier in a table
choices.why: Delete the row and every copy of the value is worthless.

choices.text: A token in local storage
choices.why: Clearing a local copy leaves any other copy working.

choices.text: A cookie with a short lifetime
choices.why: The browser drops its copy, and the credential itself was never revoked.

prompt: A team measures their site with the cache disabled in the developer tools. What is wrong with the number they get?
hint: Ask who experiences that.

choices.text: It is the first-visit number
choices.why: A site measured that way is a site nobody actually loads.

choices.text: It is optimistic about the time
choices.why: It is pessimistic: everything is fetched rather than served from disk.

choices.text: It is unusable; compression is off
choices.why: It disables neither compression nor anything else about the transfer.

choices.text: It is right for mobile visitors
choices.why: Mobile browsers hold caches like any other.

prompt: A service worker was shipped with a defect and now serves a broken page from its own store. Why is this worse than an ordinary bad deploy?
hint: Ask whether the affected browsers are asking you anything.

choices.text: It runs before the page does
choices.why: True of the ordering, and not what makes recovery hard.

choices.text: Your code in their browser, asking nothing
choices.why: Sites have shipped a deliberate self-uninstalling version to recover.

choices.text: It gets a far larger store than an ordinary cache
choices.why: Size is not the difficulty; reachability is.

choices.text: It is installed per tab
choices.why: One registration covers the site rather than one per tab.
